item.title: A new role isn’t a new process
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Leaders picked design engineer as the next core role while half of teams changed nothing about how design gets approved.
item.content:encoded:
Leaders are answering AI with a change to the roster instead of a change to who approves work, and the collaboration numbers show the roster change doesn’t fix what broke.

Ask design leaders what the ideal product team looks like now and a job title shows up that most orgs didn’t have two years ago. In AI in Design 2026, among the leaders who didn’t select “product designer” as a core role, 72% selected “design engineer” and 44% selected “AI design specialist.” Designer Fund and Foundation Capital surveyed more than 900 designers across 60 countries for it.

The instinct is sound. Designing a screen and building it have collapsed into one motion on a lot of teams, and somebody has to be good at both ends of that.

Then you read the structure question in the same report. Half of respondents, executives and managers and individual contributors alike, say their teams haven’t made significant structural changes. Only 7% added new AI-focused roles.

So the design engineer is the stated ideal of a field that has mostly changed nothing. The gap between those two answers is the interesting part, and it isn’t a budget story.

The receipt is in the collaboration numbers

A third of respondents, 34%, say collaboration has become messier, with roles and ownership less clearly defined than before. Twenty percent say collaboration has decreased outright. In 2025 that number was 5%.

Four times worse in a year. Whatever that is, it didn’t happen because designers got worse at talking to engineers.

The cause isn’t mysterious. The work picked up more authors and nobody moved the ownership to match. “Roles and ownership less clearly defined” is the respondents’ own language, and it describes a definition problem rather than a skill problem.

The capability already spread

One number should settle whether a title is the fix. Half of all respondents have pushed AI-generated code to production, product and brand designers included. Only 20% identify as design engineers.

The hybrid work is already being done by people whose job description says something else. Hiring a design engineer on top of that doesn’t change who ships. It gives one person a title for work half the field is doing without one.

It also tells everyone else their job didn’t change. The AI work routes to the person hired for it, every other role definition stays exactly as it was, and the new capability sits with one hire who can take it with them.

What DoorDash changed instead

Shali Nguyen, head of consumer experience design at DoorDash, describes the other move in the same report. Their pull request process stayed as it was. “Everything goes through GitHub PR approvals, and designers are held to the same production-quality bar as our engineering counterparts.” Then they added one thing: “We’ve added a design review step where designers are tagged to review and approve UI changes before they go to production.”

No new role. A named approval, bolted onto a step that already existed, with designers answerable to the same bar as the engineers next to them.

That’s what a structural change looks like once it’s written down. It survives a resignation. It applies to everyone who touches the surface, including the product manager who generated a screen on Tuesday afternoon.

What I ask before opening a role

When someone brings me the case for a new kind of designer, I ask which approval is currently unowned. Not which skill is missing. Which decision gets made today by nobody in particular.

There’s usually an answer, and it’s a step rather than a person. Then the real question is whose name goes on that step and what standard they hold the work to, and I can write that down this week without a requisition.

The trade I work from is that the team owns the method and I own the standard and the decision. The method turns over every quarter now. The standard shouldn’t, because the standard is the part you can hand to somebody who wasn’t in the room.

The cleanest version of that I’ve done is the whole-library audit at Best Egg. I built and ran it across 296 files, wrote the crawler’s rules and directed the remediation. Writing the rules was the actual work. A rule precise enough for a crawler to apply is a standard that no longer needs me sitting in the review. A senior product designer on the team ran the button component audit end to end, agent and remediation, and that one was hers.

Where the title earns its place

The DesignWhine editorial team, writing in April, calls the AI design engineer “a high-value specialization, not a universal career direction” and ties demand for it to specific conditions: a high cost to translate design into code, or AI features built into the product itself. That’s the honest version of the case. Under those conditions I’d hire for it.

What the role can’t do is settle ownership. A specialist makes the hybrid work better where there’s a lot of it. A specialist doesn’t decide who signs off on a screen a product manager generated last night, and that’s the part 34% of the field says got worse.

Adding a role is the half of this problem a leader can solve in a budget conversation. Changing who approves what means editing job descriptions, review steps and somebody’s authority, and that one makes people unhappy in meetings.

Seven percent of teams added the role. Half changed nothing about how work gets approved. The collaboration numbers moved anyway, in the wrong direction, and a title on an org chart has no approval step attached to it.

item.title: The summary dropped the user who disagreed
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Researchers trust AI most for summarizing. Across 18 models, bias against minority views ran 34.4 times larger than random. The objection goes first.
item.content:encoded:
The argument about AI in research is policing the participant and leaving the summary alone, and summarization is the step that drops the one user who disagreed.

On October 5 Jakob Nielsen gave the synthetic-user argument its cleanest form. Use AI personas to open up the problem, then put real people in front of the thing before you ship it. He called it syntheticipation and wrote the rule as “Diverge with silicon; validate with carbon.”

He’s right, and he has the receipts for it. When Nielsen Norman Group ran synthetic users against three studies they had already done with real people, the synthetic answers came back agreeable and flat. A real learner said “I didn’t finish all the courses.” The synthetic one said “I completed all the courses I mentioned.” Nielsen’s conclusion from it is “Real users are meaner. Cherish that.”

So the rule guards one door. It decides who answers the questions. It doesn’t say anything about who writes up the answers.

The fight is over the part almost nobody uses

User Interviews surveyed 150 research professionals in May. Eight percent actively use tools that simulate participants. 28% reject the idea outright and 47% call themselves skeptical and want more evidence first.

In the same survey, 80% said they use AI regularly in their work. Maze asked nearly 500 researchers and product people over the new year and found 69% using AI on at least some research projects, up 19 points in a year.

Read those together. The loud argument is about a tool fewer than one in ten researchers has adopted. The quiet default, already in most studies, is a model reading the transcripts and telling you what’s in them.

Trust peaks exactly where it shouldn’t

Lyssna asked 300 practitioners how much they trust AI across the synthesis tasks. Trust falls as the task takes more interpretation: 82.9% for summarizing, down to 25.6% for visualization.

That ranking makes sense if summarizing is compression. It isn’t. Summarizing is selection, and something has to be left out for the summary to be shorter than the thing it summarizes. What matters is what gets cut, and that has now been measured.

What a summary does to an objection

A study published in March benchmarked 18 language models on aggregating opinions and scored how well each summary represented the people in the source. Minority views lost. Bias against them ran 34.4 times larger than random bias, consistently, across every model and every topic they tested. The paper separates people who see themselves as a minority from positions that are semantically in the minority, and finds both under-represented in the generated summaries.

A January paper by Aghaebe and colleagues names the mechanism. Summarizers resolve disagreement while they write. Handed a set of people who don’t agree, the model converges on the dominant view and the dissent comes out the other side as consensus.

The failure here isn’t inaccuracy. The summary is accurate about the majority. The problem is that the one person who said the thing nobody else said is the cheapest line to cut, and that person is usually the reason the study was worth running.

On the Cross-Sell work at Best Egg, applicant interviews before design started turned up this, from someone who had just been declined: “I probably won’t use you again. It made me mad and frustrated.” One person, one sentence, and it set the shape of the work. I put it in the before-state flow next to the dead end and it’s still on the case study. A good themed summary would have filed it under negative sentiment at decline. True, and nothing to design from.

The quote that argues against the recommendation

When a team brings me a synthesis, I ask for the strongest quote that argues against the recommendation. Not the limitations slide. A sentence a real person said that makes the recommendation harder to make.

If nobody can produce one, I don’t assume the finding is wrong. I assume nobody has checked whether the disagreement survived the write-up, and the study goes back until someone has looked. Usually the objection is sitting in a transcript nobody reopened. The check costs an afternoon, because the raw material never left the building.

The same question works in an interview. Not whether a candidate uses the research tools, which everyone does now, but what the inconvenient finding in their last study was and what they did about it.

Where the rule needs extending

Validating with carbon and writing up with silicon gets you a study with real people in it and a deliverable that reads like agreement. The participants were real. The disagreement died in the summary, and the team acted on the summary.

So extend the rule one step past the participant. The objection belongs in the synthesis, in the words the person used, with the recommendation it cuts against named next to it. If it isn’t in there, the study isn’t finished, however many real humans sat for it.

item.title: Explainability ends on the decline screen
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: The guidance saying a checkbox isn’t a reason was withdrawn in May 2025. Regulation B still lets a denial notice say ‘length of residence.’
item.content:encoded:
Explainability gets built as a property of the model and delivered as a string on a screen, and Regulation B’s floor for that string is a label with no direction and no size.

The standard answer to AI underwriting right now is per-feature attribution. Compute each applicant’s contribution scores, rank them, map the top few onto reason codes. That beats the older habit of back-filling a plausible reason from the application form after a score came back, and the people building it aren’t wrong.

It stops one step short of the applicant. The notice is the only part of a credit model a denied person will ever read, and Regulation B lets it be a noun.

The playbooks cite guidance that’s gone

A compliance guide dated May 1, 2026 opens by saying that “CFPB Circulars 2023-03 and 2024-06 require specific, accurate reasons for every adverse action.” Circular 2023-03 was withdrawn on May 12, 2025. So was 2024-06, which covered hiring and employment screening rather than credit. Both went out in one Federal Register notice that withdrew 67 guidance documents at once.

Circular 2022-03 went with them, and that’s the one worth missing. It asked whether a creditor using algorithms complex enough to obscure the reasons still owes the applicant specific ones, and answered that “ECOA and Regulation B do not permit creditors to use complex algorithms when doing so means they cannot provide the specific and accurate reasons for adverse actions.” Its page is still up at the original address. You would have to read the Federal Register to know it no longer applies.

The Bureau’s most recent circular is 2024-07, from December 2024. The notice put its reasoning as removing compliance obligations imposed outside notice-and-comment rulemaking. Whatever you make of that, the documents telling lenders a checkbox isn’t a reason are no longer operative, and at least some 2026 compliance writing still cites them as binding.

What the regulation still asks for

ECOA didn’t change and neither did Regulation B. Section 1002.9(b)(2) requires a statement of reasons that is “specific and indicate the principal reason(s) for the adverse action.” It closes the two easy exits: a creditor can’t point at internal standards or at a failing score.

The official commentary is where the ceiling sits. On quantity, the regulation “does not mandate that a specific number of reasons be disclosed, but disclosure of more than four reasons is not likely to be helpful to the applicant.” On depth, it gives an example. “A creditor need not describe how or why a factor adversely affected an applicant. For example, the notice may say ‘length of residence’ rather than ‘too short a period of residence.‘”

The compliant floor is four nouns, accurate to what the model actually scored, carrying no direction and no size. Length of residence. Someone reading that can’t tell whether they’d lived somewhere too briefly or too long, or whether it shaved a few points off or decided the entire application. A model can be fully interpretable and still produce that notice, because the notice gets written somewhere else by someone else.

The screen isn’t the notice

Here’s the distinction the explainability work skips. The adverse action notice is a formal document on a 30-day clock. The screen where a person finds out is a different artifact, and Regulation B has nothing to say about it.

Best Egg’s decline screen read “Unfortunately, we are unable to approve your application at this time.” Every declined applicant left the funnel there. On Cross-Sell we replaced that dead end with a secured loan offer for the people who qualified, which came to about $40M in Home Secured and $3.7M in Vehicle Equity originations.

I raise it for the sequence, not the number. The applicant reads the screen first and forms a view of what happened. The notice arrives days later, to a person who already decided. Different teams own those two surfaces at most lenders, and neither one treats the pair as a single explanation.

Where this is still enforced

In July 2025 the Massachusetts attorney general settled with Earnest Operations, a student lender, for $2.5 million. The coverage went to the model, fairly. There was a knockout rule that denied applicants on immigration status and a Cohort Default Rate variable that fell harder on Black and Hispanic applicants.

The notices were in there too. Ballard Spahr’s summary of the allegations lists “inaccurate adverse action notices that prevented applicants from understanding their own creditworthiness.” That isn’t a modeling finding. An inaccurate notice is a string that doesn’t match what the system did, which makes it a content and interface problem that ended up inside a $2.5 million settlement.

What I ask for

Before I’ll take a lender’s explainability story seriously I ask for two things: the full list of reason strings the system can send, and how often each one fires. Not the model card. The strings.

A ranked attribution that terminates in a list nobody has opened since the integration shipped explains nothing. If no one in the room owns that list, the interpretability work is decoration. The string that fires most often is the one to rewrite first, because it’s the sentence the largest number of declined people are going to read.

Federal guidance saying a checkbox isn’t a reason has been gone since May 2025. Regulation B still permits “length of residence.” Everything a denied applicant understands above that floor is a design decision, and at most lenders it’s being made by whoever wrote the strings first.

item.title: Getting hands-on costs you the crit
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Managers already spend a median 40% of the week on individual contributor work. The advice to get hands-on with AI tools comes out of the crit.
item.content:encoded:
Hands-on time with agents comes out of the feedback hours, and feedback is the only part of the week that holds up as a team gets bigger.

The advice going to design leaders this year is to get your hands back on the tools. Katie Dill, head of design at Stripe, puts it plainly in AI in Design 2026: “If leaders want to understand what’s actually possible and how their teams need to adapt, they have to get close to the makers and hands-on with the tools themselves.”

She’s right, and I’d go further. A design leader who hasn’t built anything with an agent is guessing about the work their team does all day, and the guess shows up in the standard they hold.

The question nobody attaches to the advice is which hours it replaces.

The second job was already there

Gallup put the question to a random sample of 16,442 American managers and leaders. Ninety-seven percent said they carry individual contributor work on top of leading people. The median manager spends 40% of the week on it.

So getting hands-on isn’t a new allocation. It’s a bigger share of a half that was already full.

The same study carries the number being passed around this fall. The average team went from 10.9 direct reports in 2024 to 12.1 in 2025, nearly 50% larger than when Gallup first measured in 2013. The median held at five or six. The average moved because the big teams got bigger, not because every manager woke up with more people.

Span isn’t the variable

Chris Cancialosi made that case well on September 29. Writing about the flattening, he argues that span of control “is not an independent variable. It is a multiplier on a condition set somewhere else.” The condition is the individual contributor load. A manager with four reports and a full delivery queue is in worse shape than one with 14 reports and nothing to build.

His fix goes to human resources. Screen managers on two numbers, team size and estimated time on non-managerial work, then intervene where both run high.

That fix assumes somebody assigned the work. In design, increasingly, nobody did.

The leader picked it up. An agent made producing look free, so the thing that used to take a designer a week now looks like an afternoon on the leader’s own calendar. It doesn’t feel like taking on delivery work. No screen catches it either, because on paper it isn’t a delivery queue. It’s curiosity, and the field is telling leaders to have more of it.

What comes off the calendar instead

The report that carries Dill’s advice also tells teams to “run crits more often, in smaller groups. Shorter, more frequent sessions mean that feedback happens while the work is still in progress.” One team in the study went from weekly crits to 4x weekly crits across sub-groups.

Read those two recommendations next to each other. Both are good. Both are drawn on the same week, and only one of them has a meeting invite with other people’s names on it.

That asymmetry decides which one survives a bad month. Prototyping with an agent is work a leader can do at 9pm with nobody noticing it moved. A crit that gets skipped is visible to eight people, which is exactly why it’s the first thing a leader quietly stops defending when their own build queue fills up. Nobody announces it. The invite stays on the calendar and the quality of what happens inside it drops.

The one finding I’d plan around

Gallup’s most useful result isn’t about team size at all. About seven in 10 employees were highly engaged regardless of team size when they strongly agreed they had received meaningful feedback.

Regardless of team size. Feedback is the part of the job that keeps working at 14 reports. Hands-on tool time is the part that doesn’t scale with anything, because it only ever informs one person.

Manager engagement fell from 27% to 22% between 2024 and 2025, the sharpest year over year drop Gallup has recorded, and nine points below where it sat in 2022. Those are the people now being told to add a build practice.

How I spend the week

Most of my week goes into feedback. Weekly reviews, structured critique and time on specific work with specific people. I’d rather give a little every week than a lot at once, because feedback that arrives in a batch arrives after the decision.

On the cross-sell work there were two products, two roadmaps and two release calendars. I ran the weekly reviews for both myself so the patterns stayed shared across them. That was the expensive choice and it was the right one.

I do the hands-on part too. I built and ran the whole-library audit at Best Egg across 296 files, wrote the crawler’s rules and directed the remediation, which was weeks of my own hands on an agent. I scheduled it around the reviews rather than through them. A senior product designer on the team ran the button component audit end to end, agent and remediation, and that was hers.

Here’s the check I’d run this quarter. Count the hours you spent producing last month against the hours you spent giving feedback, then ask which of the two numbers you’d defend to your team out loud.

What the advice is missing

Get hands-on. The advice is right and the people giving it are right about why. What it leaves out is the trade, and the trade is bad. You learn the tools faster, and your team gets less of the one thing Gallup found holds engagement at any team size.

Ninety-seven percent of managers had a second job before agents made the second job look easy. The hours for the new advice come from somewhere, and the crit is the softest thing on the calendar.

item.title: Generated screens still need a record
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: A Google banking prototype scored 84.38 on usability against 53.96 for the fixed app. The protocol that ships those screens keeps no copy of them.
item.content:encoded:
When the interface is assembled per person at runtime, the record of what was rendered becomes part of the design deliverable, because support, review and accountability all need two people looking at the same screen.

Michael Bernstein published a two-page vision paper for UIST last month arguing that interfaces are about to stop being durable things. Software construction is getting cheap enough that we’ll build them at the moment of need instead, which he calls “rapid, discardable, on-demand interfaces tailored to our needs in the moment”. When you’re finished with one, you “tear the interface away like a used sheet of paper, and start your next task on a blank one.”

He takes the obvious objection seriously inside the paper. Just-in-time interfaces break Nielsen’s consistency heuristic, and Microsoft already rolled back adaptive menus once because people couldn’t predict them. His bet is that usefulness wins anyway, the way file sharing won despite terrible affordances. I think he’s probably right, and familiarity is the objection everybody reaches for first.

It’s the sentence about us that should stop a design leader.

we create the levers that shape what gets created and how they operate, but we may never lay hands or eyes on the last-mile interfaces themselves

Michael S. Bernstein, The Interface of Theseus, September 2026

That’s an operations sentence, not a philosophical one. If the designer never lays eyes on the screen that shipped, no one else does either, and the screen is gone by the time anyone wants to discuss it.

The strongest demo was a bank

This isn’t a thought experiment waiting on better models. Google Research ran a within-subject study with 72 participants on Penny, a digital banking prototype, comparing an adaptive generative version against a fixed one. The adaptive version scored 84.38 on the System Usability Scale against 53.96, a gap of 30 points. The authors put it down to cutting what they call the navigation tax.

A separate Google team showed the generation itself holds up. Yaniv Leviathan and 11 colleagues found that generated interfaces are overwhelmingly preferred over the markdown wall of text an LLM normally returns, and at least comparable to expert-crafted work in half of cases. Trond Wuellner has been making the practitioner case for shipping this since May.

So the evidence is real, it’s good, and the place it was measured most convincingly is a banking app, where every screen in the product is a disclosure of some kind.

The record is already in the transport

The fix is cheaper than the problem sounds, because of how these screens travel.

A2UI, the protocol Google opened up for agent-driven interfaces, doesn’t ship code to the client. The agent sends a JSON payload carrying a component tree and its data model, and the client maps that onto its own native widgets. The screen exists as a document before it exists as pixels. Every generated interface in that architecture is already serialized, already small and already passing through a server.

Neither the protocol’s own introduction nor Google’s launch post says anything about storing it, logging it or replaying it. Both are about getting the screen rendered correctly and safely, which is the right job for a spec. What happened afterward is left to whoever builds the client, and right now the default is that it’s gone.

Finance already requires reproduction

The E-Sign Act has had an answer to this since 2000. Under 15 U.S.C. 7001(d)(1), an electronic record kept to satisfy a retention requirement has to accurately reflect the information and stay accessible “in a form that is capable of being accurately reproduced for later reference”.

A rate, a fee schedule or a repayment term assembled for one person at one moment and then thrown away isn’t capable of being reproduced for later reference. It isn’t a design preference that the bank keeps a copy. It’s the condition on doing it electronically at all.

What I ask in a review

When a team brings me a surface that a model composes, the question I ask isn’t whether we can explain the model. It’s what the person taking the call sees when this customer calls back about this screen.

That question has a way of settling arguments fast. If the answer is a transcript, or a reconstruction, or a confident guess from a dashboard, the design isn’t finished no matter how well it tested.

On the document verification work at Best Egg, applicants who had uploaded their files couldn’t tell what was pending, so they called to ask. We gave each document a status they could see, and the verification rate went to 71% against 61% for control in the live A/B test, sized with product and operations at 7,000 fewer support calls a month. The screen was fixed, so the applicant and the agent on the phone were at least describing the same thing. Take that away and the call starts with both people guessing.

Two halves of one deliverable

If Bernstein’s equilibrium shift lands the way he describes it, the design deliverable splits in two.

The first half is the one the field is already building: the catalog, the rules, the signals, the evaluation criteria. The generator. That work is underway and A2UI’s trusted component catalog is a good version of it.

The second half barely has a name yet. It’s the record of what the generator actually produced for a given person at a given moment, kept long enough and structured well enough that a support agent, a reviewer, an accessibility audit or a regulator can put it back on screen. Not analytics about the session. The session’s interface, re-renderable.

Designers are good at arguing for the first half, because it looks like design. The second half reads like a storage bill, so it lands on an engineering backlog and stays there. It’s worth more than that. It’s what makes a generated screen something a company can stand behind after the fact.

The JSON that drew the screen is sitting in the transport layer already. Throwing it away is a decision, and at the moment it’s the one being made by default.

item.title: Revoking an agent doesn’t cancel what’s pending
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Six banks and a bill in Congress agree an agent’s access must be revocable at any time. Neither says what the screen tells you when you use it.
item.content:encoded:
Revoking an agent stops the next authorization. It doesn’t cancel what the agent already set in motion, and the screen where a person turns an agent off is the only place that could tell them the difference.

On September 22 six banks published a shared set of principles for trusted agentic commerce: NatWest, ASB Bank, Bank of America, Capital One, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and ING. Hans Overeem, who runs payments at ING, put the point plainly. “As AI agents enter the payments ecosystem, customers must remain in control, understand what the agent is doing, and have confidence that their data and payments are secure.”

A week before that, Mike Lawler and Josh Gottheimer introduced the Stop Rogue AI Act, which hands NIST the job of writing standards so an organization can “allow, deny, or revoke an agent’s access, actions, and interactions at any time, so people have the final say over what it can access or do.”

This is the one thing the whole industry agrees on, and it’s correct. Revocation has to be there.

Both documents treat it as a capability. A capability is something a system has. Revoking is something a person does, at a particular second, usually because they’re alarmed, and what they need at that second is not a switch.

Authorization and the purchase come apart

A team at Southern University of Science and Technology, the Indian Institute of Technology and City University of Hong Kong modeled four agent payment protocols in Tamarin at the end of August: x402, the Machine Payments Protocol, the Agentic Commerce Protocol and AP2. Across 86 verification cases they turned up 40 findings that hadn’t been documented before. One sentence in their introduction explains why this is hard, and it’s about sequence rather than cryptography.

“A user may authorize a task before the final merchant or terms are fixed, so each subsequent step can be locally valid while the transaction as a whole is inconsistent with that authorization.”

Read that as a calendar. The person grants authority on Monday. The agent picks the merchant on Wednesday, the money moves Thursday and the box arrives the week after. Revoking on Wednesday evening lands in the middle of that, and which parts it reaches depends on plumbing the person can’t see.

The specs are detailed about the front of that sequence. AP2’s core concepts give the Intent Mandate a list of authorized payment methods, the shopping criteria and an expiration time. Taking it back isn’t on the page. Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol announcement, from October 14, 2025, is about how a merchant recognizes an agent it can trust. The consumer’s side of revocation isn’t in it either.

Identity already wrote this down

RFC 7009 is the OAuth token revocation spec, and it’s honest in a way product copy never is. “The invalidation takes place immediately, and the token cannot be used again after the revocation.” Then, a few lines later: “In practice, there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not.”

It goes further. “If the authorization server does not support access token revocation, access tokens will not be immediately invalidated when the corresponding refresh token is revoked.” Pull the thing that issues access and the access it already issued can keep working.

That has been in the spec for years, in the plumbing agent payments are built on. The difference now is that the token spends money.

The revoke that counts is the bank’s

There’s also a legal answer to where the switch belongs, and it’s older than any of this. Regulation E says a transfer isn’t unauthorized when it was initiated by “a person who was furnished the access device to the consumer’s account by the consumer, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that transfers by that person are no longer authorized.”

Everything turns on that last clause. The revocation that changes a person’s position is the one their bank hears about. Switching the agent off inside the agent’s own app, which is where a person would obviously go to do it, is housekeeping.

Six systems out of 21

Alexandra Michael and Franziska Roesner at the University of Washington reviewed 21 agent permission systems proposed between 2024 and 2026, plus five commercial agents. Their finding on this point is blunt. Of the 21, “only six clearly provide ways for users to change or revoke permissions after the policy has been specified,” and two of those six only allow the change between sessions rather than during one.

They name the assumption underneath it. These systems “assume that a one-time decision extrapolates to all future circumstances.”

They’re writing about agents in general, not payments. Payments is where that assumption carries a dollar amount.

What the screen owes a person

Visa’s own research found about half of respondents worried about “decisions made without me.” Asked whether they’d still use a shopping agent without control over their data, 54% said not very or not at all likely. Those were online surveys of card holders who shop online monthly: 1,600 in the United States, 1,600 in Australia and 500 in New Zealand.

A revoke screen that says “Access removed” answers a question about the system. The questions a person actually has are about their money, and there are four. What did my agent already commit me to? Which of those does this switch stop? Which of them is still coming anyway? Where do I go to cancel each one?

That’s a list, and lists are generated from state somebody has to go and fetch: orders placed and not shipped, an authorization approved yesterday that posts on Friday, the subscription the agent started under its own credential at the merchant. None of it is exotic. It just isn’t anybody’s ticket, because the feature shipped when the grant screen worked.

So in any review where a screen hands something authority, I ask to see the second screen in the same session. Not the confirmation. The one where a person takes the authority back, and what it lists when they land on it. The first screen is usually in high fidelity. The second one is usually a line in a backlog.

At Chainlink Labs I directed Staking v0.1, and the call I made there was about where the facts sit. The pool gauge, the reward rate and the remaining allotment went next to the stake action, so nobody had to leave the page to decide.

Charlie Liu, writing Agentic Commerce Daily on October 2, summed up the week as trust and payment infrastructure “hardening around continuous authorization and open standards.” That’s a fair read of what’s being built. Continuous authorization means the grant keeps working while nobody is watching it, which makes the moment somebody wants it to stop more consequential.

The switch most products will ship lives in the agent’s app, because that’s where the agent lives. Regulation E puts the one that changes a person’s legal position at their bank. Somebody is going to decide which of those a person gets, and on current evidence it’s whoever owns the settings page.

item.title: Promote on decisions you wrote down
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: 67% of companies tie promotion to AI skills. Designers say they can’t fully account for their own output, so the evidence has to be recorded early.
item.content:encoded:
A rubric line for AI skills adds a competency to the ladder without replacing the evidence the ladder lost, and the only fix is writing the decision down when it gets made.

Sixty-seven percent of organizations now link AI skills to promotion criteria. Half tie them straight to performance ratings. Both numbers come from HiBob’s 2026 AI skills research, which surveyed 1,200 decision makers across six regions in February and March.

In design the change has a face. An executive at a publicly traded company told the AI in Design 2026 survey that every design role now has AI craft skills in the rubric, “built into our mid-year and annual review cycles to measure where in the percentile each employee sits relative to peers in these new craft skills.” Meta did it at scale first. Janelle Gale, its head of people, told staff last November that AI-driven impact becomes “a core expectation” from 2026.

I don’t think any of that is unreasonable. A leader who watches the work change this fast and leaves the ladder untouched is pretending nothing happened.

The part the rubric doesn’t touch

HiBob’s own write-up in Charter, published September 22, names the gap this way: “AI skills are entering performance reviews before many companies have defined what ‘good’ actually looks like.” The proposed fix is clearer standards.

Define the competency better and you still have the older problem underneath it. A performance review is an evidence exercise. You read the work, you read your notes, you decide. The work used to carry authorship on its face. It doesn’t now.

Designers say so themselves, in the same AI in Design survey. Forty percent call the direction and judgment fully theirs. Another 43% say the work is mostly theirs while they’re aware AI shaped outcomes they didn’t fully control. Nine percent say it’s “genuinely hard to separate” their contribution from the tool’s.

Read that as a measurement problem rather than an identity one. When the person who made the file isn’t sure which parts were their call, a manager opening that file eight months later is not going to recover it.

Someone already named this

Keyuri Anand wrote the sharpest line on it in August: “Your promotion did not disappear. The evidence you used to earn it did.” She calls it the proxy collapsing. Polished artifacts stopped signaling judgment because they got cheap.

Her advice goes to the designer. Own a system, stop shipping tasks, build something that proves judgment. That’s good advice and it’s aimed at the wrong person. A designer can’t fix the evidence base a company promotes from. The manager owns that, and right now the manager is being handed a new rubric line and the same broken packet.

Tommy Geoco made the structural version of this point at UX Tools last week. Writing about design career ladders, he argues that most technology panic “isn’t about the tool. It’s about what happens when the old path to competence disappears before anyone builds a new one.” The path up was also the path along which a manager could watch someone’s judgment develop. Both of them went at the same time.

The behavior they ranked first

The same research has a finding that didn’t travel. Asked which everyday AI behaviors matter most, decision makers put two at the top, tied at 52%: proactively reviewing output quality, and documenting workflow decisions.

So the field already knows what it needs. Neither of those is a proficiency. Both are records. You can’t percentile-rank someone on documenting workflow decisions, which is probably why 67% of organizations wired promotion to AI skills instead.

One more finding from the same research. Only 36% of organizations that expect managers to build AI capability see those managers as highly prepared to do it.

What my review notes carry now

I run weekly design reviews, and what changed is what leaves the meeting written down. The call, the reason it went that way and the name of the person who made it. Not the file. The decision.

It takes four or five lines. The reason I bother is that a promotion case assembled in November from work done in March is a reconstruction, and a reconstruction favors whoever talks about their work most fluently. Notes taken at the time favor whoever was right.

At Best Egg I wrote the crawler’s rules for the whole-library audit before the agent touched a file, across 296 files. Those rules are the artifact that shows what I thought good meant. The 28 fixes a run produced show that the agent worked. Separately, a senior product designer on the team ran the button component audit start to finish, agent and remediation, and that sentence is in my notes because in eight months the files won’t say it.

The 13% who changed something

Betterworks surveyed 2,387 HR leaders, managers and employees this year and found executives six times more likely than employees to believe performance reviews and goal setting have kept up with AI-driven work. In the same study 49% of HR leaders rank AI use as a top influence on performance. Nine percent of employees think it matters to their success.

That spread is what a rubric change looks like from underneath. The line gets added, the cycle runs, and the people being measured can’t tell what it bought them.

In design, 13% of leaders have updated official performance review metrics or hiring practices at all. The ones who did mostly added a skill. The evidence their reviews run on hasn’t changed, and it no longer records who decided what.

item.title: A design review can’t see accessibility
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: WebAIM found WCAG failures on 95.9% of a million home pages and 56.1 errors on the average one. Those defects don’t show up in a screenshot.
item.content:encoded:
Accessibility defects are invisible to the review designers actually run, so the control has to be a check that runs on every build against rules someone wrote down.

The standard answer to generated interfaces is review. A model writes the screen, someone looks at it before it ships, and the bar holds because a person was in the loop.

That works for the defects a person can see.

In February, WebAIM ran its yearly scan of a million home pages. It found detected WCAG failures on 95.9% of them, up from 94.8% a year earlier, and 56.1 errors on the average page, up 10.1%. Nearly every one of those pages belongs to a team that would tell you it reviews its work.

What looking can’t find

Focus order. Accessible names on icon buttons. Whether a modal traps focus or drops the keyboard behind it. Contrast ratios. An error state carried by a red border and nothing else.

Writing on DEV on September 26, a developer publishing as LXSAIHUB worked through the mechanism: those are the defects that survive a screenshot and survive a code review read at normal speed. Their dashboard example is three icon buttons with no accessible name, a button wrapped around an SVG and nothing else.

None of that is a judgment call. It’s a set of facts about the markup, and a person looking at a rendered screen has no way to check any of them. Color, hierarchy, copy and layout review fine from a screenshot. Everything in the list above needs a keyboard or a script.

Mikhail Prosmitskiy made the engineering version of this argument in Smashing Magazine on June 30. Accessibility is an operational capability, like reliability or security, and models produce inaccessible markup by default. He’s right, and the tooling he points at is the right tooling. The part his piece doesn’t have to deal with is that a lot of this markup no longer arrives through engineering at all.

The markup for a screen increasingly comes out of a tool a designer is driving, and designers brought a review method with them that was built for pictures. It’s a good method. It catches the things it was built to catch. It has never had a step where somebody touches a keyboard, because it never needed one.

The tool’s explanation isn’t the build

There’s a second failure underneath. If you can’t see the defect, the reasonable fallback is to read what the tool says it did.

A paper submitted on July 24 by Kashif Imteyaz and five co-authors benchmarked exactly that. They ran 24 UI generation tasks across five generative UI tools, 120 interfaces in total, and compared each stated design rationale against the interface that actually came out.

A quarter of the rationales weren’t implemented. For functional requirements it was 34%. On average the tools recognized 54% of the UX principles written into the prompts, and four of the five implemented 6% or fewer of the functional ones. The authors call it design theater: a plausible explanation with no dependable connection to the code.

So the rationale isn’t review either. It’s a second artifact that needs checking.

The code works anyway

This isn’t a story about weak models. In April, Syed Mohammad Kashif and six colleagues had Cursor build 10 large projects, averaging 16,965 lines and 114 files each, then ran static analysis across them. Average functional correctness came in at 91%. The same projects carried 1,305 design issues by one analyzer and 3,193 by another, with accessibility among the most prevalent categories.

The code runs and the markup is wrong at the same time. A demo won’t surface that and a passing test suite won’t flag it.

A check that can fail the build

I’ve argued on this blog that the judgment in a design system is the part you can’t automate, and I still think that. This is the other case. Accessible names, focus order, contrast and landmarks are mechanical, checkable and dull, which is why leaving them to a human eye is hard to defend once the volume goes up.

At Best Egg I built and ran an audit across the whole component library. I wrote the crawler’s rules and directed the remediation that came out of it. The report wasn’t the useful part. The rules being written down was, because the same check could run again and the answer didn’t depend on who was looking that day.

That’s the shape I’d ask for: the check runs on every build and it can fail the build. Not a review-day checklist and not an audit at the end of a quarter. Prosmitskiy’s version of this is that accessibility should depend on process instead of memory.

In the review itself

In a design review I ask whoever’s presenting to put the trackpad down and tab through the screen while everyone watches. It takes about 20 seconds. It finds the focus trap, the control that announces nothing and the step you can’t reach without a mouse. Nobody enjoys it the first time.

The written standard matters more than which linter you pick. If no one on the team can say what good means for a disabled state or an error message, no tool will decide it, and whatever the model produced becomes the standard by default.

WebAIM’s scan and that static analysis run both turned these defects up with no person in the room. That’s the clearest argument available for putting the same kind of check in the pipeline and letting it stop a release.

item.title: The dispute form has no agent option
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Agent purchases get disputed under codes written for stolen cards, and Regulation E’s own definition may defeat the box a person picks.
item.content:encoded:
A card dispute gets classified by the cardholder at intake, from a fixed list, and that label decides which rules and clocks run. For an agent purchase there’s no true option on the list.

Theodore Sterling, writing at chargeback.io on August 21, 2026, named the gap in agentic commerce disputes: “Today’s tools can’t capture the mandate that proves an agent stayed inside the customer’s limits.” Three things are missing, he says. The customer’s authorization, the agent’s identity and a tamper-resistant record tying the two together.

Networks and dispute vendors are building all three. It’s the right work, and it lands one step too late.

Somebody picks the reason first

A card dispute doesn’t reach an investigator as an open question. It arrives with a label already on it. The cardholder opens the app or calls the number, and the first thing they’re asked is what kind of problem this is. Their answer becomes a reason code, and that code decides which rules run, what the merchant gets asked for and how long everyone has.

Sterling names the codes an agent purchase lands under today: “A disputed agent purchase files under a reason code you already work with, most often Visa 10.4, 13.1, or 13.3.” Other fraud in a card-absent environment. Merchandise not received. Not as described.

Now read that list as somebody whose shopping agent bought a $400 espresso machine they never asked for. The machine arrived, so it isn’t a not received claim. It’s exactly as described, so it isn’t that one either. Nobody stole the card. The only box left says a person used the card without permission, and that isn’t true, because they set the agent up themselves.

The box most people will pick

They’ll pick fraud anyway. It’s the closest thing on the list to “I didn’t want this,” and it’s the box with a trapdoor in it.

Regulation E defines an unauthorized electronic fund transfer as one “initiated by a person other than the consumer without actual authority to initiate the transfer and from which the consumer receives no benefit.” It then excludes a transfer initiated by “a person who was furnished the access device to the consumer’s account by the consumer, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that transfers by that person are no longer authorized.”

You furnished the access device. On purpose, to your agent, in a setup flow that almost certainly called it connecting your card.

Whether that exclusion reaches software at all is unsettled. Eli Clemens argued at ITIF on March 23, 2026 that Regulation E “provides no clear framework for how to handle disputes in agentic commerce,” and that the CFPB should say plainly that “consumer-authorized agents do not waive all error resolution rights.” Nobody has said it yet. So the person at the intake screen is making a legal argument they don’t know they’re making, by tapping the least wrong option on a menu.

The clock starts at the statement

The timing rules don’t help either. Under 1005.11 the notice has to reach the institution “no later than 60 days after the institution sends the periodic statement.” The bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or up to 45 if it puts a provisional credit on the account, and up to 90 for point-of-sale debit claims.

Those clocks run from the statement date, not from the day the person noticed. An agent buying quietly through a month gets most of that window before anyone reads a line of it.

Amex built a second path

One network has done something a customer can actually see. American Express commits that “if a Card Member authorizes a registered AI agent to make a purchase, and that agent sends American Express the customer’s authenticated purchase intent, American Express will protect eligible customers from charges related to AI agent error.” It says that protection sits “in addition to ordinary course dispute resolution processes.”

That’s a real commitment, and it tells you something. Amex built a second path because the first one has nowhere to put this. Look at the conditions too: a registered agent, and authenticated intent that actually got sent. Miss either one and the customer is back at the reason list with everyone else.

What I look at first

On any product where money can go wrong, I ask to see the list of reasons a person can pick from when they report a problem, before I look at the flow being demoed. That list is short, usually inherited, and usually owned by nobody in the room. It’s also the only place a person gets to say what happened to them, and everything downstream is decided by which line they tap.

If the true reason isn’t on the list, the product has decided that problem doesn’t exist.

I’ve watched what a screen with no honest option does to people. At Best Egg the decline page told applicants their application couldn’t be approved and stopped there. One of them told us in an interview, “I probably won’t use you again. It made me mad and frustrated.” The fix wasn’t better wording. I set a cross-sell framework for the funnel, and the team replaced “Rejected” with a few questions about the vehicle, so a declined applicant could say something about their situation and get a secured offer instead of a dead end.

The mandate record is worth building, and it’ll get read after a case that was already sorted into the wrong pile by someone choosing from three options, none of which described what happened. That list is a design surface. Right now it’s inherited from a world where the only thing that went wrong was a stolen card.

item.title: The bottleneck moved and the budget didn’t
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Developers and engineering leaders both name reviewing AI output as their top constraint. Teams are spending the gain on deferred hires instead.
item.content:encoded:
When agents triple a team’s output the constraint moves to the people who decide whether the work is right, and spending that gain on a deferred hire funds the queue instead of the decision.

On September 25, Dan Graves, chief product officer at WitnessAI, published an account of how his product team works now. Seven people, each managing a role-based agent with subagents under it. A product design agent called Muffin turns mockups into working code. An orchestrator called PacMan routes tickets. Release velocity doubled. By the team’s own weekly measure, interfaces designed, each user experience designer now produces what three used to.

It’s the most specific writeup of an agent-run product team I’ve read this year, and he’s candid about what broke. Muffin’s early designs “looked right on the surface but used the wrong components and missed our branding”, and developers reworked half the output. A senior designer picked “finish the load animations” off a list of options just to point Muffin at the task, and Muffin started building. That’s a real account, not a case study with the failures sanded off.

The sentence I keep going back to sits in the middle of it. “We’ve since automated the path from specification to ship, which only moved the constraint. The human reviewers are now the bottleneck.”

Then he says where the money went

Further down the same piece: “Together, these gains have let us defer hiring new staff.”

He’s right on both counts, and the two point opposite ways. The team found its constraint and then spent the surplus everywhere except on it. Output at the designer level went up three times. The number of people who can look at that output and say no stayed at seven.

I don’t read that as carelessness. It’s what a throughput gain feels like from the inside. The queue gets longer at the last step, which is the least visible place for it to get longer, and the savings from not hiring land this quarter while the cost of a thin review lands in something that ships wrong two quarters from now.

It isn’t one team’s problem

Two days before that piece ran, Qodo published a Censuswide survey of 500 American software developers and 300 American engineering leaders, all at companies where AI already does real work in the development lifecycle. The two groups answered separate questionnaires and never saw each other’s answers. Asked to name the primary constraint in their delivery pipeline, both picked reviewing and validating AI-generated code, at 26% each. It outranked trusting the output, integration, security and compliance, context retrieval and cost in both samples.

Two audiences with different incentives, one answer. The report’s line for it is that “generation scaled across the entire lifecycle, and verification never scaled with it”. In the same research, 89% of organizations reported an AI-related production incident, and 3.7% of engineering leaders said their current processes are enough to hold quality as agents take on more work.

That’s engineering data. The design version is on the same curve now, because design output goes into the same pipeline. When an agent hands a reviewer finished frontend code with the mockups attached, the reviewer’s problem is the one those 800 people just described.

Teaching agents to out-review humans

Graves’s answer to his own bottleneck is to push the review down to the agents. His team aggregates everyone’s review questions into a checklist the agents run every time, then asks Claude for other industry review practices and teaches those too. “Eventually, an agent reviews things 100 ways automatically, leaving less that requires a human eye.”

Half of that is right and it’s the half nobody should be arguing with. If a check can be written down as a rule, a person should never run it twice. Component use, contrast, the naming, whether the empty state was drawn at all: that work belongs to an agent running at three in the morning.

The other half files a hundred checks and one decision under the same word. A checklist can tell you the screen conforms. It can’t tell you the screen shouldn’t exist, that the flow asks an applicant for a document they won’t have on a Sunday, or that the answer is correct and still wrong for this customer. Automating the first job doesn’t create capacity for the second. It clears the desk faster and leaves the same people holding the part that was always scarce.

The hire you already paid for

Box’s 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise surveyed 1,640 information technology decision makers across the United States, United Kingdom, France and Japan in early May. 58% expect headcount to rise over the next three years. Among the most mature adopters, 79% do. The companies furthest into this are not the ones planning to be smaller.

So deferring a hire is a choice, and it deserves to be argued as one. A team that triples its output has earned the case for another person who can decide. Making that case is harder than banking the saving, because the deferred hire is a line a finance partner can see and a thin review is not.

How I plan a team now

I size a team by what it can decide in a week rather than what it can produce. When I ran the whole-library audit of Best Egg’s design system, the plan divided at write access: specs and lists to the agent, every edit to the library to one senior product designer, and the order set by who could act. The agent was never the constraint. One read-only run produced 28 fixes with deep links into Figma. Write access was the constraint, and we built the schedule around it instead of finding out later.

Before anyone on my team adds an agent, I ask two things. Who signs this off, and what else is already on that person’s desk. If the answer is someone already at capacity, the agent isn’t adding throughput. It’s adding a queue with their name on it.

Graves knows exactly what his agents cost. He publishes the figure: $2,000 to $5,000 per person per month. The review those agents generate doesn’t appear on any invoice, which is most of the reason it’s the easy thing to defer.

item.title: Disclose the review, not the tool
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: 58% of creatives have used AI on client work without saying so. The label they’re all arguing about carries a penalty and no information.
item.content:encoded:
Naming the tool isn’t a quality signal, because the same disclosure penalty lands on a master and a beginner. What a client can act on is the record of what was checked and what came back wrong, and no disclosure policy asks anyone to write that down.

Nielsen Norman Group published a framework last week for deciding when to tell people AI was involved in your work. Taylor Dykes calls it PACED: policy, audience, context, expectations and degree of use.

It’s careful work and it names the awkward part honestly. People say they want disclosure and then think less of the person who gives it.

I’d use that framework tomorrow. I also think the question underneath it’s set up wrong, and a good framework built on a bad question inherits the problem.

“AI was used here” is a fact about a tool. Nobody on the receiving end is asking about the tool.

The label costs something and says nothing

Envato surveyed 1,780 creative professionals for Beyond Adoption. Fifty-eight percent have used AI on client work without telling the client. Only 31% always disclose.

The more interesting number is the reason. Of the people who said nothing, 48% said they don’t see why they should have to disclose every tool. That gets read as a rationalization. It’s half right.

Nobody itemizes Figma, the stock license, the plugin or the Slack thread where the idea actually came from. A tool name has never told a client whether the work is any good.

And the penalty for saying this particular tool name is measurable. Dykes cites the studies: ratings drop as the disclosed share of AI involvement goes up. The research Florida International University wrote up from Joel Carnevale, Anand Benegal and Lynne Vincent is the part that should stop people. Listeners marked a composition down when they were told AI was involved, and the hit landed whether they believed the piece came from Hans Zimmer or from a first-year music student.

The same penalty fell on a master and a beginner.

A signal that can’t tell those two apart isn’t carrying information about the work. It’s carrying a reaction to a category, and we’re building policy on top of it.

Provenance is not review

Article 50 of the EU AI Act became applicable on August 2, 2026. Synthetic audio, image, video and text have to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. Deepfakes get disclosed. A chatbot has to say what it is.

That’s provenance and it’s worth having. It answers whether a machine made the pixels, which is a real question for a voice in an ad or a face in a video.

It doesn’t answer the question a client, a reviewer or a design lead is actually asking. That question is whether anyone competent looked at this, and what they were looking for.

The review is happening off the books

In AI in Design 2026, the survey Designer Fund and Foundation Capital ran with 900 designers across 60 countries, 80% say they rely on their own quality judgment over the model’s. Half have pushed AI-generated code to production. Forty percent claim full ownership of AI-assisted work and another 43% say it’s mostly theirs.

So the review exists. It happens in one person’s head, it takes real skill, and it leaves nothing behind that anybody else can inspect.

Patrick Neeman got close to this in Craft Still Matters, arguing that you describe your standards and keep humans reviewing. What I’d add is that the describing has to land somewhere a reader can find it.

What I write instead

Nothing I hand over carries the words “AI-assisted”. The line I write instead says what I checked and what came back wrong.

Three sentences, at the top, before the work: here’s what I checked this against, here’s where it failed, here’s what I changed. If I can’t write those three sentences, naming the tool doesn’t rescue the handoff, and naming the tool is the only thing most disclosure policies ask me for.

I ran a whole-library audit at Best Egg and wrote the crawler’s rules myself. The rules are the reason anyone could argue with the output. A flag was checkable because the rule behind it was on paper, which meant the interesting conversation was about the rule and not about the crawler.

In an interview I ask for one piece of work and the thing the model got wrong on it. Not whether they use the tools. What the first answer was, why they threw it out and what they held it up against. A candidate who can’t answer that has been shipping unreviewed work, and no disclosure label would have told me.

Who stays quiet, and why

Dykes is right that being caught out hurts more than telling people yourself, and that’s a good reason to disclose when policy is pointed at you. It’s also why disclosure gets heard as a confession. A confession is a bad container for a claim about quality.

The Envato rates break along exposure. Agency and studio owners disclose least at 28%, behind freelancers at 31% and in-house designers at 35%. Europe is highest at 39% and the Middle East and Africa lowest at 22%.

The people with the most staff and the most to lose say the least. That’s what a label looks like when it carries risk and no upside.

You don’t fix that with a better decision tree about when to say the word. You fix it by changing what gets said, from a fact about the tool to a record of the judgment. A record gets more useful as the tools spread. The tool name is heading for describing everything, and a label that describes everything sorts nothing.

Fifty-eight percent are already not saying it. Arguing them into compliance is a smaller win than it looks. What a client can act on is the check, and not one of the frameworks in this argument asks anyone to write the check down.

item.title: A name match is not a verdict
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Europe just updated its payee name check and the UK wants to keep its own for good. A match confirms the name. Banks are printing verified.
item.content:encoded:
A payee name check answers one narrow question, and the screen reporting it’s where a bank quietly answers a much bigger one on the payer’s behalf.

On September 20 the European Payments Council’s Verification of Payee rulebook moved to version 1.1. It was an urgent release, fixing problems that surfaced once the service went live.

In Britain the Payment Systems Regulator is consulting on removing the expiry date from the direction that requires Confirmation of Payee, so the rule doesn’t lapse on 1 November. In the US the Federal Reserve sells banks Payee Name Verification, which checks a name against a routing and account number before the money goes.

The shared position is reasonable: checking the name on the account is fraud prevention. It is, for one kind of fraud. The trouble starts with the word the screen uses to report it.

The check does what it says

Uptake isn’t in question. Over 320 payment service providers offer the check in the UK, more than 99% of firms initiating a Faster Payment now offer it, and over 2 million checks complete every day.

It works. Pay.UK found a 59% drop in claims for payments sent to the wrong account, and losses down between 20% and 40% for some types of fraud. The regulator adds that a transaction where the name doesn’t match is 25 times more likely to be fraudulent.

A mismatch is one of the strongest single signals in retail payments. The check surfaces it before the money moves, which is why I’m not arguing against it.

What a match cannot tell you

The PSR’s own account of the rule is careful about the distinction. Confirmation of Payee “was introduced to stop misdirected payments”. Then: “There was also an expectation that it would reduce the number of authorised push payment (APP) scams.”

The first happened. The second hasn’t shown up in the totals. UK Finance reported £576.4 million lost to authorized push payment fraud in 2025, up 19%, across 248,070 cases. Banks reimbursed £354.3 million of it, about 61%.

No causal claim there. The reason the check can’t reach those scams is in the mechanism, not the rollout.

The check compares the name the payer typed with the name on the account. When someone is being talked into a payment, the same person supplies both. The fake seller gives you the name on the real account they control. The invoice arrives with new details on a letterhead you know. Both sides of the comparison come from the fraudster, so the check agrees with them.

The Federal Reserve is careful about this in its own marketing copy. Its service “may help to reduce the occurrences of Authorized Push Payment fraud where an imposter is impersonating an individual”. May help. Impersonating an individual. That’s one scam, not the category.

The rulebook stops at the screen

The European rulebook runs to 68 pages and it’s precise where it needs to be. A responding provider returns one of five outcomes: match, no match, close match with the counterparty’s actual name, identification code not supported or verification not possible.

Then it says this about the person: “It should be noted that the way the Requester is informed and the content of the notification messages are left to the discretion of the Requesting PSP.”

So the machine-to-machine part is specified to the field. The part a human reads is a matter of taste. Sixty-eight pages on the message, one sentence on the screen.

The wording carries the liability

This isn’t a copy quibble, because the European regulation already attached money to that screen. On a mismatch the payer’s provider must say that authorizing the transfer “might lead to transferring the funds to a payment account not held by the payee indicated by the payer”.

The provider also may not stop the payer going ahead. And it has to explain “the implications for PSP liability and PSU refund rights resulting from a decision by PSUs to ignore a notification”.

Read that in order. The bank warns you, can’t stop you, and your refund rights change if you continue. The sentence deciding all of that’s being written by whoever owns the string file.

Two things I would hold the screen to

The first is a labeling rule. A check gets named for what it checked, so “this account is in the name you typed” is true and boring. “Payee verified” is a claim about the payment, and it’s the screen a fraudster wants glowing behind their phone call. A name check is a fact about an account, not a judgment about a person.

The second is the no-match state, which needs something to do. Today, in RedCompass Labs’ summary of European go-live, the payer “can either proceed, amend, or stop the payment altogether”. Three doors and no help choosing between them, at the exact moment somebody may be on the phone explaining which one to pick.

My question in review is always the same. What can this person do in the next 10 seconds, and does the screen still work if they’re being coached while they read it?

I got that from the expensive end. At Best Egg I redesigned document verification so an applicant sees a status the moment a file lands, and the opportunity we sized was 7,000 fewer support calls a month. A status that doesn’t say what happens next produces a phone call. On a payment screen it produces a payment.

At Auth0 the same lesson arrived in a different vocabulary. A check that returns true is an engineering result. Turning it into “verified” is a product decision, and it’s usually made by nobody in particular.

Europe will run this check on every euro credit transfer. Britain looks set to keep its version for good, and the Fed is selling one by the transaction. None of the three specifies what the payer reads. That leaves the most load-bearing word in the flow to whoever writes it, which today is a designer working without a rulebook.

item.title: Count the drift, not the adoption rate
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: Design system buy-in fell from 42% to 32% in a year. Teams are told to build a business case from a return only 5% of them measure.
item.content:encoded:
A design system team earns its staffing on the count of what the system failed to prevent, not on an adoption rate or an estimate of hours saved.

Satisfaction with stakeholder buy-in for design systems fell to 32% this year, down from 42%. The share of practitioners calling themselves dissatisfied went from 23% to 40%. Both numbers come from zeroheight’s fifth annual report, which surveyed 147 people who run a design system.

In the same survey, 56% named a lack of resourcing or staffing as their biggest problem. So the people holding the budget are less convinced than they were, and the teams have fewer people than they need.

The answer the field reached for

The field’s answer is to get better at the business case. Figma’s new business case for design systems, published in January, argues that systems “have evolved from static libraries to key drivers of business revenue, customer loyalty, and product strategy”. It comes with receipts. Freshworks cut customer service costs 28%. Grammarly saved its design and development teams 25% of a work week.

That’s a fair position. I’d rather a design system lead walked into a budget review talking about revenue than about component counts.

The trouble is sitting in the other half of the zeroheight report. Only 5% of teams measure return on investment at all. Just 41% track adoption. The field is being told to argue from evidence most of it has never collected.

So the case gets built out of somebody else’s numbers. Freshworks did the work and published it, and the slide borrows it. Nobody in your finance review is funding your team on Grammarly’s week.

The hours nobody followed

Shane P Williams put the sharpest version of this on September 14. Teams are good at counting the hours a system gives back and bad at saying where those hours went. “Two thousand reclaimed hours is only a win if you can name what they bought,” he writes. If they went into shipping more of the same, faster, “then what the system funded is volume”.

He’s right, and I’d push it one step further back. Most teams can’t name what the hours bought because they never had the hours. The saving came out of a spreadsheet, not a measurement.

And when a team does go and measure, the first number they reach for is the one that hides the problem.

Adoption rate is a flattering number

Adoption answers one question: are people using our components. That’s the number a system team hopes to see, which is most of the reason it gets picked.

It’s also the number the tools hand you. The report found measurement scattered across Figma analytics, surveys, code repository tracking and spreadsheets, with 37% of teams using Figma analytics. Adoption is what comes out of the box, so adoption is what gets reported.

When I measured our library at Best Egg, adoption came back at 90.7% across 1.15 million instances in 296 files. Read on its own, that number says the work is finished.

The same audit found 844,333 values hand-set in files where a published token was sitting right there, unwired. It found 770 components with zero instances. Half the standalone library turned out to be illustrations that every designer scrolls past on the way to a button.

Adoption was 90.7% and the library still cost the team something every day. One of those numbers is an argument for leaving us alone. The other is an argument for funding us.

Count the drift

Drift is what the system failed to prevent. It’s countable, and it’s the only design system number I have watched change a staffing conversation.

  • Hand-set values that already have a token. Every one is a decision the system was supposed to have made for somebody.
  • Components with no instances. Maintenance you pay for that sits unused.
  • Ties the data can’t break. The value 10px appeared 1,834 times in our files and 12px 1,796. Nothing in the counts picks one. A person has to, and that person costs money.

A number like 844,333 does something an adoption rate can’t. It hands the person holding the budget a quantity they can multiply by a cost, and it names the work that would bring it down.

Make the number harder to like

My test for a measurement is whether it can embarrass me.

Ours nearly wasn’t. The adoption formula had a name-match heuristic in it, counting a layer as on-system when its name looked close enough to a real component. I took it out. I excluded the archives and the library’s own file, and reported Brand Studio separately, because marketing collateral doesn’t instance a dropdown.

Every one of those choices pushed my own number down. That’s the point. An adoption rate that only ever goes up is a marketing asset, and the people reading it can tell.

The other half of the test is the calendar. The audit runs again on the first of every month, so drift has a trend and not a snapshot. One reading is a claim. Twelve of them is a line on a chart, and a line is what survives a budget review full of people who don’t design.

Where the 56% comes from

Put the two findings next to each other. Resourcing is the top challenge, named by 56% of teams. Return on investment is measured by 5%.

Those are the same fact. Design system teams are asking for headcount in a currency they never minted. The business case advice isn’t wrong. It’s out of order. Instrument the thing, find out what it’s failing to prevent, and the case is yours instead of borrowed.

Seven percent of the teams in that survey report full adoption. Another 22% say the system reaches few teams. Somewhere in the gap between those two lines is a number with a dollar sign on it, and only about one team in 20 has gone and counted it.

item.title: Prototypes that cannot fail are demos
item.dc:creator: John DeSouza
item.description: 43% of companies expect a working prototype as the deliverable. A deliverable gets approved. A prototype is supposed to be able to come back wrong.
item.content:encoded:
The cost of a high fidelity prototype used to force a team to name the question before the build. Now that the cost is gone, the question has to be written down on purpose, or the prototype is just a demo with a review on the calendar.

Jakob Nielsen made the case in Vibe Coding and Vibe Design, quoting a line from Kshitij Agrawal that the field has more or less adopted.

mockups existed because coding was difficult; now that coding is easy, the future is prototypes

Kshitij Agrawal, quoted by Jakob Nielsen, March 2025

Go straight to something that runs. Test the real interaction instead of a picture of it. I agree with all of that. The conclusion skips a step, and the step it skips is the one that made prototypes work.

A high fidelity prototype used to cost about a week of somebody’s time. That price did a job nobody assigned to it. It forced a conversation before the build, because no team spends a week without asking what the week is for. The question came first because the budget made it come first.

The deliverable ate the question

Forty-three percent of designers say their company now expects a working prototype as the deliverable, according to AI in Design 2026, a survey of more than 900 designers in 60 countries. Half have pushed AI-generated code to production. In the State of Prototyping survey run by Tommy Geoco and UX Tools, 1,478 responses collected this spring, 43.8% now spend more than half their building time on code a model wrote.

A deliverable and a prototype have different jobs. A deliverable gets accepted. A prototype gets built to be wrong in a particular way that somebody named in advance, and the whole point is that it might come back wrong.

When the artifact arrives before the question, the question gets written afterward, if anyone writes it at all. A question written after the build is a rationalization with a sample size attached.

What gets approved is average
